paragraphs: Given that women are educated in the enervating manner recommended by the writers I have been criticizing, and that their subordinate place in society gives them no chance to recover the ground they have lost, is it any wonder that everywhere they appear to be a defect in nature? When we consider how decisively an early association of ideas shapes the character, is it any wonder that they neglect their understandings and give all their attention to their persons?

The great advantages that naturally follow from stocking the mind with knowledge are obvious from the following considerations. The association of our ideas is either habitual or instantaneous, and the latter kind seems to depend on the original temperament of the mind rather than on the will. Once ideas and matters of fact have been taken in, they lie in reserve until some chance circumstance makes information received at very different periods of our lives dart into the mind with illuminating force. Many recollections are like a flash of lightning, one idea assimilating and explaining another with astonishing speed. I am not now referring to that quick perception of truth which is so intuitive that it defies investigation, and leaves us at a loss to decide whether it is memory or reasoning, lost to sight in its swiftness, that opens the dark cloud. Over those instantaneous associations we have little power; for once the mind has been enlarged by wide-ranging flights or deep reflection, the raw materials will, to some degree, arrange themselves of their own accord. The understanding, it is true, may keep us from drawing out of proportion when we group our thoughts, or when we copy the warm sketches of fancy from the imagination; but the animal spirits, the individual character, supply the colouring. Over this subtle electric fluid,* how little power we have, and how little power reason can gain over it! These fine, intractable spirits seem to be the essence of genius, and, beaming in its eagle eye, they produce in the highest degree that happy energy of associating thoughts which surprises, delights and instructs. These are the glowing minds that concentrate pictures for their fellow creatures, forcing them to view with interest objects, reflected from the impassioned imagination, which they had passed over in nature.

(*Footnote. Sometimes, when in the mood to laugh at materialists, I have asked whether — since the most powerful effects in nature seem to be produced by fluids, the magnetic, etc. — the passions might not be fine volatile fluids enveloping humanity and holding its more refractory elementary parts together, or whether they were simply a liquid fire running through the more sluggish materials and giving them life and heat?)

Let me explain myself. Most people are unable to see or feel poetically; lacking imagination, they run from solitude in search of things their senses can grasp. But once an author lends them his eyes, they can see as he saw and take pleasure in images that lay before them but that they could not have singled out.

Education, then, only supplies the man of genius with knowledge that gives variety and contrast to his associations. But there is a habitual association of ideas, which grows “with our growth,” that has a great effect on the moral character of mankind, and which gives the mind a bent that usually remains throughout life. The understanding is so pliable, and yet so stubborn, that associations formed by chance circumstances during the years in which the body grows to maturity can seldom be disentangled by reason. One idea calls up another, its old associate, and memory, faithful to first impressions, especially when the intellectual powers are not employed to cool our sensations, retraces them with mechanical exactness.

Such habitual slavery to first impressions does more harm to the female character than to the male, since business and other dry work of the understanding tends to deaden the feelings and to break up associations that do violence to reason. Females, however, are made women while still mere children, and then brought back to childhood just when they ought to leave the baby-walker behind for good; so they lack the strength of mind to wipe away the artificial layers under which nature has been smothered.

Whatever they see or hear serves to fix impressions, stir emotions and link ideas in ways that give their minds a sexual character. Mistaken notions of beauty and delicacy stunt the growth of their limbs, producing a sickly tenderness instead of fineness of organs. Weakened like this, because they spend their energy unfolding the first associations that everything around them forces on them rather than examining them, how are they to gain the vigour required to throw off their artificial character? — where will they find the strength to turn back to reason and rise above a system of oppression that blights the fair promise of spring? This cruel association of ideas, which every influence conspires to weave into all their habits of thought — or, more precisely, of feeling — grows stronger once they begin to act a little on their own; for they then discover that pleasure and power are to be had only through their skill in arousing emotions in men. Moreover, every book written expressly to instruct them, making the first impression on their minds, instils the same opinions. Since they are educated in a bondage worse than Egypt’s, to reproach them for faults they can scarcely avoid is as unreasonable as it is cruel — unless we assume in them a native vigour that falls to the lot of very few among mankind.

The harshest sarcasms, for instance, have been directed at the sex, and women have been mocked for repeating “a set of phrases learnt by rote,” though nothing could be more natural, considering how they are educated, and that their “highest praise is to obey, unargued” — the will of man. If they are not granted reason enough to govern their own conduct — why, then everything they learn has to be learned by rote! And since all their ingenuity is spent on arranging their dress, “a passion for a scarlet coat” is so natural that it has never surprised me. And if we grant that Pope’s summary of their character is just, “that every woman is at heart a rake,” why should they be harshly condemned for looking for a kindred mind and preferring a rake to a man of sense?

Rakes know how to play on their sensibility, whereas the modest merit of reasonable men naturally affects their feelings less; such men cannot reach women’s hearts through the understanding, since the two have few sentiments in common.

To expect women to be more reasonable than men in their LIKINGS, while still denying them the free use of reason, seems a little absurd. When do men FALL IN LOVE with good sense? When do they, with all their superior powers and advantages, turn from the person to the mind? How can they then expect women — taught only to watch behaviour and to acquire manners rather than morals — to despise what they have toiled all their lives to attain? Where are women suddenly to find the judgment to weigh patiently the good sense of an awkward but virtuous man, whose manners, which they have been trained to judge critically, repel them, and whose conversation seems cold and dull because it is not made up of pretty repartees and well-turned compliments? If we are to admire or esteem anything for long, our curiosity must at least be roused by some knowledge of what we admire; we cannot judge the worth of qualities and virtues that lie beyond our comprehension. Such respect, where it is felt, may be very sublime, and the confused awareness of her own humility may, from some points of view, make the dependent creature an interesting object; but human love needs coarser ingredients, and the person will quite naturally claim its share — and it mostly claims an ample one!

Love is largely an arbitrary passion; like certain other stalking mischiefs, it rules by its own authority and does not deign to reason. It is also easily told apart from esteem, the foundation of friendship, because fleeting beauties and graces often arouse it — although, to give the feeling energy, something more solid must deepen their impression and set the imagination working, to make the fairest — the first good.

Ordinary qualities arouse ordinary passions. What men look for is beauty and the simper of good-humoured docility; what captivates women is an easy manner. A gentlemanly man seldom fails to please them; their thirsty ears eagerly drink in the insinuating nothings of politeness, while they turn from the unintelligible sounds of the charmer — reason, charm he never so wisely. In superficial accomplishments the rake certainly has the advantage, and of these women are able to judge, for this is their own ground. Since the whole tenor of their lives has made them gay and giddy, the mere look of wisdom, or the severe graces of virtue, must seem gloomy to them and impose a kind of restraint against which they — and love, that playful child — naturally rebel. Lacking taste, except of the lighter sort — for taste is born of judgment — how are they to discover that true beauty and grace must spring from the play of the mind? And how can anyone expect them to value in a lover what they themselves lack, or have only very imperfectly? In them the sympathy that joins hearts and invites confidence is so faint that it cannot catch fire and rise into passion. No, I say it again: the love such minds cherish must feed on coarser fuel!

The conclusion is plain. Until women are led to use their understandings, they should not be mocked for being attached to rakes, or even for being rakes at heart, since this seems the inevitable result of their education. Those whose life is to please must find their enjoyment, their happiness, in pleasure! It is a trite remark, but a true one, that we never do anything well unless we love it for its own sake.

Suppose for a moment, however, that at some future turn of time women were to become what I sincerely wish them to be: even love would then gain a more serious dignity and be refined in its own fires, and, as virtue lent true delicacy to their affections, they would turn from a rake in disgust. Reasoning as well as feeling — for feeling is at present woman’s only province — they could then easily guard themselves against outward graces, and they would soon learn to despise a sensibility that had been aroused, and made stale, among women whose trade was vice and by the wanton airs of allurement. They would bear in mind that the flame (one has to use the proper expressions) which they hoped to kindle had been burned out by lust, and that the sated appetite, having lost its taste for pure and simple pleasures, could be stirred only by the licentious arts of variety. What satisfaction could a woman of delicacy expect from a union with such a man, when the very guilelessness of her affection might strike him as insipid? Dryden describes the situation thus:
“Where love is duty on the female side, On theirs mere sensual gust, and sought with surly pride.”

But there is one great truth that women have yet to learn, though it matters greatly to them that they act on it. In choosing a husband they should not be led astray by the qualities of a lover — for a husband, even supposing him to be wise and virtuous, cannot long remain a lover.

If women were educated more rationally, and could take a more comprehensive view of things, they would be content to love only once in their lives, and after marriage calmly let passion subside into friendship — into that tender intimacy which is the best refuge from care, yet which is built on such pure, still affections that idle jealousies would not be allowed to disturb the discharge of the sober duties of life, nor to take up thoughts that ought to be employed otherwise. This is a state in which many men live, but few, very few, women. And the difference can easily be accounted for without resorting to a character peculiar to their sex. Men, for whom, we are told, women were made, have occupied women’s thoughts too much; and this association has so entangled love with all their motives of action that — to harp a little on an old string — having been employed solely either in preparing themselves to excite love or in actually putting their lessons into practice, they cannot live without love. But when a sense of duty, or fear of shame, obliges them to restrain this pampered desire to please beyond certain lengths — too far for delicacy, it is true, though far from criminality — they obstinately resolve to love their husbands (I speak of their passion) to the end of the chapter; and then, acting the part which they foolishly demanded of their lovers, they become abject wooers and doting slaves.

Men of wit and fancy are often rakes, and fancy is what love feeds on. Such men will inspire passion. In its present childish state, half the sex would pine for a Lovelace — so witty, so graceful, so brave a man; and do they DESERVE blame for acting on principles that are drummed into them so constantly? They want a lover and a protector — and there he kneels before them: bravery prostrate before beauty! So love pushes a husband’s virtues into the background, and bright hopes or lively emotions keep reflection at bay until the day of reckoning — which will surely come, turning the sprightly lover into a surly, suspicious tyrant who treats with contempt the very weakness he encouraged. Or suppose the rake reformed: old habits are not quickly shed. When a man of ability is first swept away by his passions, sentiment and taste are needed to varnish the enormities of vice and give zest to brutal indulgences; but once the gloss of novelty wears off and pleasure palls upon the senses, lasciviousness shows its bare face, and enjoyment is reduced to the desperate effort of weakness fleeing from reflection as from a legion of devils. Oh, virtue, you are no empty name! All that life can give — you give!

If much comfort cannot be expected from the friendship of a reformed rake of superior abilities, what follows when he lacks sense as well as principles? Truly, misery in its most hideous form. When the habits of weak people have been hardened by time, reform is barely possible, and it actually makes those beings miserable who have not mind enough to be amused by innocent pleasure. Like the tradesman who retires from the bustle of business, they find that nature presents them with nothing but a universal blank, and their restless thoughts prey on their dampened spirits. Their reformation, like his retirement, actually makes them wretched, because it deprives them of all employment by quenching the hopes and fears that set their sluggish minds in motion.

If habit has such force, if folly holds us in such bondage, then how carefully we should guard the mind from storing up vicious associations! And we should take equal care to cultivate the understanding, to rescue the poor creature from the weak, dependent condition of even harmless ignorance. For only the right use of reason makes us independent of everything — except the unclouded Reason, “Whose service is perfect freedom.”
